questions.prompt: The four 'cardinal' virtues -- so called because all other human virtues hinge on them -- are prudence, justice, fortitude, and:

questions.correctAnswer: Temperance
questions.explanation: 'Cardinal' comes from the Latin cardo, 'hinge.' These four virtues, acquired by human effort and habit, are the hinges on which a well-ordered moral life turns.
questions.hint: It's the virtue of self-moderation, keeping desires within due limits.

citations.quote: 'Cardinal' comes from the Latin 'cardo,' hinge -- these four virtues are the hinges on which the rest of the moral life turns.

questions.prompt: 'Prudence,' as a cardinal virtue, means:
choices: Right practical judgment about what to actually do in a given situation
Timid caution that avoids all risk
Raw intelligence or high IQ
Following rules without thinking about them
questions.correctAnswer: Right practical judgment about what to actually do in a given situation
questions.explanation: Prudence isn't timidity -- it's the virtue that lets a person correctly discern the true good in a concrete situation and choose the right means to reach it.
questions.hint: It's about applying good judgment to a real decision, not just being smart in the abstract.

citations.quote: Prudence is the virtue that disposes practical reason to discern our true good in every circumstance and to choose the right means of achieving it.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Fortitude,' as a cardinal virtue, means feeling no fear at all.
questions.explanation: Fortitude is firmness in pursuing the good despite difficulty, danger, or fear -- not the absence of fear. It means acting rightly in spite of fear, not never feeling it.
questions.hint: A person can feel afraid and still have this virtue, as long as they act rightly anyway.

citations.quote: Fortitude is the moral virtue that ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good... to conquer fear, even fear of death.

questions.prompt: The cardinal virtue of '____' ensures the will's mastery over instincts and keeps the desire for pleasures within due limits.
questions.correctAnswer: temperance
questions.explanation: Temperance doesn't mean suppressing every desire -- it means keeping legitimate desires (for food, drink, and other goods) rightly ordered rather than letting them run unchecked.
questions.hint: It is the virtue that moderates the desire for pleasures.

citations.quote: Temperance is the moral virtue that moderates the attraction of pleasures and provides balance in the use of created goods.

questions.explanation: Justice orders our relationships toward the common good, respecting the rights of others and fulfilling our duties toward God and neighbor alike.

questions.explanation: This is the working distinction that matters: cardinal virtues are built the way any skill is built, through repetition, while the theological virtues are put directly into the soul by God. questions.prompt: True or False: The Beatitudes describe an impossible ideal that no person could live, since CCC 1717 teaches they describe an abstract theoretical standard rather than an achievable pattern of life.
questions.explanation: CCC 1717 teaches the Beatitudes depict the very countenance of Jesus Christ himself and describe a way of life made possible by grace, not by unaided human effort -- 'impossible ideal' objections miss that these describe a real, lived pattern of holiness, genuinely attainable in Christ and through his grace, rather than an abstract theory no one could ever embody.
questions.hint: CCC 1717 ties the Beatitudes to an actual person's real character, not a theoretical standard.

citations.quote: The Beatitudes depict the countenance of Jesus Christ and portray his charity.

questions.prompt: Which is the best example of a concrete weekly resolution that names a specific Beatitude and the vice it counters?
choices: 'This week I will practice poverty of spirit by giving away something I don't need, countering the pull of avarice'
'This week I will avoid thinking about virtue altogether'
'This week I will focus only on avoiding all risk of any kind, regardless of the situation'
'This week I will measure my holiness only by how I feel emotionally each day'
questions.correctAnswer: 'This week I will practice poverty of spirit by giving away something I don't need, countering the pull of avarice'
questions.explanation: This is the model of a good resolution: naming a specific Beatitude (poverty of spirit), a specific concrete action (giving something away), and the specific vice it counters (avarice) -- a doable resolution rather than a vague sentiment about wanting to be more virtuous in general.
questions.hint: The strongest resolution names a specific Beatitude, a specific action, and the specific vice it counters -- not a vague general intention.

citations.quote: Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and bids them 'renounce all that [they have]' for his sake and that of the Gospel.

questions.prompt: 'Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness' (Matthew 5:6) integrates which combination of virtues and vices?
choices: The cardinal virtue of justice, intensified by the theological virtue of hope for its full establishment, and disciplined against the vice of sloth that would let the hunger fade
Only the cardinal virtue of temperance
Only the capital vice of gluttony, negated
Only the gift of fear of the Lord
questions.correctAnswer: The cardinal virtue of justice, intensified by the theological virtue of hope for its full establishment, and disciplined against the vice of sloth that would let the hunger fade
questions.explanation: This Beatitude is not simply justice restated; the hunger and thirst language names a longing intensity beyond ordinary moral effort, sustained by hope that justice will ultimately be established, and threatened by exactly the spiritual weariness sloth names.
questions.hint: Ask what sustains a hunger over time, and what would extinguish it.

questions.prompt: Aquinas maps 'Blessed are the meek' to the gift of piety. What is the connecting logic?
choices: Piety disposes a person to right reverence toward God and others as owed a debt of honor, which is precisely what restrains anger into meekness rather than retaliation
Piety and meekness share no real connection and the mapping is arbitrary
Meekness is simply the absence of the gift of fortitude
Piety concerns only ritual observance, unrelated to temperament
questions.correctAnswer: Piety disposes a person to right reverence toward God and others as owed a debt of honor, which is precisely what restrains anger into meekness rather than retaliation
questions.explanation: Piety, in this technical sense, is reverence toward those to whom something is owed — God first, but also parents, country, and by extension anyone owed basic honor. That reverence is what tempers the impulse to retaliate, producing meekness rather than mere passivity.
questions.hint: Ask what piety disposes a person to feel toward others, and how that would show up as temperament.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Beatitudes describe an ideal so far beyond ordinary human capacity that no one should expect to actually live any of them in an ordinary life.
questions.explanation: False, and this misreading defeats the whole point of the topic. The Beatitudes are meant to be lived, disposed toward by the cardinal virtues, enabled by the theological virtues, and made responsive by the gifts of the Spirit — a demanding integration, not an impossible one, and certainly not a merely aspirational poem.
questions.hint: Ask whether the Beatitudes are meant to be something actually livable.
